newsitem.title: USA: Republicans unveil children's health, Medicaid bill.
newsitem.headline: Republicans unveil children's health, Medicaid bill.

text.p: House Republicans aim to expand health coverage to as many as half of the nation's 10 million uninsured children through broad grants that states could use to design their own health care coverage programs, according to documents obtained Sunday.
As part of legislation to implement a five-year balanced budget deal with the White House, Republicans also plan deep cuts in Medicaid spending for hospitals that serve large numbers of the poor.
Republicans appear to have backed away from one contentious element of the budget deal.

They will not spend the full $1.5 billion expected by budget negotiators to subsidize Medicare premiums for low-income seniors who will face higher monthly charges under the budget agreement. Instead, the legislation envisions spending only part of the expected amount.
Clinton administration officials expressed some concerns about the proposal, while saying they were still trying to learn all the details.
One official said the Republicans' children health proposal appeared overly broad, allowing states to use money not just for health care but for other services.

Medicaid is the state-federal program providing health care for more than 36 million poor, elderly and disabled Americans. The budget called for $15.1 billion in five-year Medicaid cuts and $16 billion for a new childrens' health program.
Children's health care has emerged as a major political issue this year.

President Clinton's original budget called for a blend of state grants, Medicaid outreach and new benefits to laid off workers to expand coverage to up to 5 million children, although analysts said it would have reached far fewer.

Lawmakers have introduced a slew of blls calling for everything from an increase in tobacco taxes to tax credits to expand health care. Further, estimates are that as many as 3 million poor children eligible for Medicaid are not receiving benefits.
The Republican plan tracks the White House in many ways. It would provide more than $2 billion in annual grants that states would use to develop programs to expand health coverage to poor children.
States would have wide latitude to decide how to deliver care -- vouchers, managed care, direct aid or other methods.

Governors could use some of the money to expand Medicaid health coverage to children, including children in families with incomes up to 150 percent of the poverty line -- about $25,000 for a family of four.

The bill would let states keep children on the Medicaid rolls for an entire year, rather than having to recertify them periodically, which could help hundreds of thousands of children retain Medicaid coverage.

The legislation would save more than $15 billion over five years largely by cutting federal payments to hospitals with many poor patients, based on a complex formula that attempts to even out the cuts nationwide. Savings are also anticipated through management reforms in the Medicaid program.
To give states more control over Medicaid spending, the legislation would make it easier to enroll poor people in managed care programs without federal approval.

The bill would repeal the so-called Boren amendment, which requires states to pay reasonable costs for long-term care. Governors have long sought relief from that provision which they say has driven up the cost of care.
The bill continues federal Medicaid payements to disabled children who lost disability aid under a new welfare law.
